{{Short description|Axiomatic set theory proposed by Wilhelm Ackermann}}
{{About|the mathematical theory of sets||Ackermann (disambiguation)}}
In [[mathematics]] and [[logic]], '''Ackermann set theory''' (AST, also known as <math>A^*/V</math><ref>A. Lévy, ''A hierarchy of formulas in set theory'' (1974), p.69. Memoirs of the American Mathematical Society no. 57</ref>) is an axiomatic [[set theory]] proposed by [[Wilhelm Ackermann]] in 1956.<ref name=AckermannOriginal>{{cite journal |last1=Ackermann |first1=Wilhelm |author-link=Wilhelm Ackermann |date=August 1956 |title=Zur Axiomatik der Mengenlehre |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF01350103 |journal=Mathematische Annalen |volume=131 |issue=4 |pages=336–345 |doi=10.1007/BF01350103 |s2cid=120876778 |access-date=9 September 2022|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

AST differs from [[Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory]] (ZF) in that it allows [[Class (set theory)|proper classes]], that is, objects that are not sets, including a class of all sets.
It replaces several of the standard ZF axioms for constructing new sets with a principle known as Ackermann's schema. Intuitively, the schema allows a new set to be constructed if it can be defined by a formula which does not refer to the class of all sets.
In its use of classes, AST differs from other alternative set theories such as [[Morse–Kelley set theory]] and [[Von Neumann–Bernays–Gödel set theory]] in that a class may be an element of another class.

William N. Reinhardt established in 1970 that AST is effectively equivalent in strength to ZF, putting it on equal foundations. In particular, AST is [[Consistency|consistent]] [[if and only if]] ZF is consistent.

== Preliminaries ==
AST is formulated in [[first-order logic]]. The [[formal language|language]] <math>L_{\{\in,V\}}</math> of AST contains one [[binary relation]] <math>\in</math> denoting [[set membership]] and one [[constant (mathematics)|constant]] <math>V</math> denoting the [[Von Neumann universe|class of all sets]]. Ackermann used a predicate <math>M</math> instead of <math>V</math>; this is equivalent as each of <math>M</math> and <math>V</math> can be defined in terms of the other.<ref name=Levy1959>{{cite journal |last1=Lévy |first1=Azriel |author-link=Azriel Lévy |date=June 1959 |title=On Ackermann's Set Theory |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2964757 |journal=The Journal of Symbolic Logic |volume=24 |issue=2 |pages=154–166 |doi=10.2307/2964757 |jstor=2964757 |s2cid=31382168 |access-date=9 September 2022|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

We will refer to elements of <math>V</math> as ''sets'', and general objects as [[Class (set theory)|classes]]. A class that is not a set is called a proper class.

== Axioms==

The following formulation is due to Reinhardt.<ref name=Reinhardt1970>{{cite journal |last1=Reinhardt |first1=William N. |date=October 1970 |title=Ackermann's set theory equals ZF |journal=Annals of Mathematical Logic |volume=2 |issue=2 |pages=189–249 |doi=10.1016/0003-4843(70)90011-2 |doi-access= }}</ref>
The five axioms include two [[axiom schema]]s.
Ackermann's original formulation included only the first four of these, omitting the [[axiom of regularity]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kanamori |first1=Akihiro |author-link=Akihiro Kanamori |date=July 2006 |title=Levy and set theory |journal=Annals of Pure and Applied Logic |volume=140 |issue=1 |pages=233–252 |doi=10.1016/j.apal.2005.09.009 |doi-access= }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/settheory-alternative/#AckeSetTheo |title=Alternative Axiomatic Set Theories |last=Holmes |first=M. Randall |date=Sep 21, 2021 |website=Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University |access-date=8 September 2022}}</ref><ref name="Fraenkel">{{cite book |last1=Fraenkel |first1=Abraham A. |author-link1=Abraham Fraenkel |last2=Bar-Hillel |first2=Yehoshua |author-link2=Yehoshua Bar-Hillel |last3=Levy |first3=Azriel |author-link3=Azriel Levy |date=December 1, 1973 |title=Foundations of Set Theory |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/bookseries/studies-in-logic-and-the-foundations-of-mathematics/vol/67/ |isbn=9780080887050 |series=Studies in Logic and the Foundations of Mathematics |volume=67 |chapter=7.7. The System of Ackermann |pages=148–153}}</ref>{{refn|group=note|Reinhardt uses A to refer to the original four axioms and A* to all five.}}

=== 1. Axiom of extensionality ===

If two classes have the same elements, then they are equal.

:<math>\forall x \; (x \in A \leftrightarrow x \in B) \to A = B.</math>

This axiom is identical to the [[axiom of extensionality]] found in many other set theories, including ZF.

=== 2. Heredity ===

Any element or a subset of a set is a set.

:<math>(x \in y \lor x \subseteq y) \land y \in V \to x \in V.</math>

=== 3. Comprehension schema ===

For any property, we can form the class of sets satisfying that property. Formally, for any formula <math>\phi</math> where <math>X</math> is not [[free variable|free]]:

:<math>\exists X \; \forall x \; (x \in X \leftrightarrow x \in V \land \phi).</math>

That is, the only restriction is that comprehension is restricted to objects in <math>V</math>. But the resulting object is not necessarily a set. 

=== 4. Ackermann's schema ===

For any formula <math>\phi</math> with free variables <math>a_1, \ldots, a_n, x</math> and no occurrences of <math>V</math>:

:<math>a_1, \ldots, a_n \in V \land \forall x \; (\phi \to x \in V) \to \exists X {\in} V \; \forall x \; (x \in X \leftrightarrow \phi).</math>

Ackermann's schema is a form of set comprehension that is unique to AST. It allows constructing a new set (not just a class) as long as we can define it by a property that ''does not refer'' to the symbol <math>V</math>. This is the principle that replaces ZF axioms such as pairing, union, and [[power set]].

=== 5. Regularity ===

Any non-empty set contains an element disjoint from itself:

:<math>\forall x \in V \; (x = \varnothing \lor \exists y (y \in x \land y \cap x = \varnothing)).</math>

Here, <math>y \cap x = \varnothing</math> is shorthand for <math>\not \exists z \; (z \in x \land z \in y)</math>. This axiom is identical to the [[axiom of regularity]] in ZF.

This axiom is conservative in the sense that without it, we can simply use comprehension (axiom schema 3) to restrict our attention to the subclass of sets that are regular.<ref name=Reinhardt1970/>

==Alternative formulations==

Ackermann's original axioms did not include regularity, and used a predicate symbol <math>M</math> instead of the constant symbol <math>V</math>.<ref name=AckermannOriginal/> We follow Lévy and Reinhardt in replacing instances of <math>Mx</math> with <math>x \in V</math>. This is equivalent because <math>M</math> can be given a definition as <math>x \in V</math>, and conversely, the set <math>V</math> can be obtained in Ackermann's original formulation by applying comprehension to the predicate <math>\phi = \text{True}</math>.<ref name=Levy1959/>

In ''axiomatic set theory,'' Ralf Schindler replaces Ackermann's schema (axiom schema 4) with the following [[reflection principle]]:
for any formula <math>\phi</math> with free variables <math>a_1, \ldots, a_n</math>,

:<math>a_1, \ldots, a_n {\in} V \to (\phi \leftrightarrow \phi^V).</math>

Here, <math>\phi^V</math> denotes the ''relativization'' of <math>\phi</math> to <math>V</math>, which replaces all [[quantifier (logic)|quantifiers]] in <math>\phi</math> of the form <math>\forall x</math> and <math>\exists x</math> by <math>\forall x {\in} V</math> and <math>\exists x {\in} V</math>, respectively.<ref>{{cite book |last=Schindler |first=Ralf |date=23 May 2014 |title=Set Theory: Exploring Independence and Truth |url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-319-06725-4_2 |publisher=Springer, Cham |pages=20–21 |isbn=978-3-319-06724-7 |chapter=Chapter 2: Axiomatic Set Theory|doi=10.1007/978-3-319-06725-4_2 }}</ref>

==Relation to Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory==
Let <math>L_{\{\in\}}</math> be the language of formulas that do not mention <math>V</math>.

In 1959, [[Azriel Lévy]] proved that if <math>\phi</math> is a formula of <math>L_{\{\in\}}</math> and AST proves <math>\phi^V</math>, then [[Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory|ZF]] proves <math>\phi</math>.<ref name=Levy1959/>

In 1970, William N. Reinhardt proved that if <math>\phi</math> is a formula of <math>L_{\{\in\}}</math> and ZF proves <math>\phi</math>, then AST proves <math>\phi^V</math>.<ref name=Reinhardt1970/>

Therefore, AST and ZF are mutually [[interpretability|interpretable]] in [[conservative extension]]s of each other. Thus they are [[equiconsistency|equiconsistent]].

A remarkable feature of AST is that, unlike [[Von Neumann–Bernays–Gödel set theory|NBG]] and its variants, a proper class can be an element of another proper class.<ref name="Fraenkel"/>

== Extensions ==

An extension of AST for [[category theory]] called ARC was developed by F.A. Muller. Muller stated that ARC "founds Cantorian set-theory as well as category-theory and therefore can pass as a founding theory of the whole of mathematics".<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Muller |first1=F. A. |date=Sep 2001 |title=Sets, Classes, and Categories |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/3541928 |journal=The British Journal for the Philosophy of Science |volume=52 |issue=3 |pages=539–573 |doi=10.1093/bjps/52.3.539 |jstor=3541928 |access-date=9 September 2022|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
